title: Before you migrate a website, save a list of every old URL (free Wayback Machine script)
author: Andy Zeng
summary: Disclosure: I build AppGripes and a small free migration page mentioned at the end. Everything else here works with free tools. This article was drafted with AI assistance; the code was tested on Oct 30, 2026. The most expensive mistake in a site migration is quiet: old URLs that used to get traffic and backlinks start returning 404 on the new site, and nobody notices for weeks. Search Console only shows you some of them, and only after Google has crawled the broken pages. The fix is boring and cheap: before you switch, write down every URL the old site ever had, then check each one against the new site and add a 301 for anything that breaks. The catch is getting that list. Your CMS knows today's pages, not the /blog/2019/old-slug from three redesigns ago that a partner still links to. The Internet Archive does know, and it has a free API for it. Step 1: list every archived URL with the Wayback CDX API The CDX server returns one row per capture. With collapse=urlkey you get one row per unique URL, and filters keep only pages that returned 200 HTML (no images, no 404s). import csv , sys , time , urllib . parse , urllib . request , json def old_urls ( domain , limit = 5000 ): """ Return unique archived URLs (status 200, HTML) for a domain from the Wayback CDX API. """ params = { " url " : f " { domain } /* " , " output " : " json " , " fl " : " original,timestamp,statuscode,mimetype " , " filter " : [ " statuscode:200 " , " mimetype:text/html " ], " collapse " : " urlkey " , # one row per unique URL " limit " : str ( limit ), } q = urllib . parse . urlencode ( params , doseq = True ) req = urllib . request . Request ( f " https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx? { q } " , headers = { " User-Agent " : " old-url-list/1.0 " }) for attempt in range ( 3 ): try : with urllib . request . urlopen ( req , timeout = 60 ) as r : rows = json . load ( r ) return rows [ 1 :] # first row is the header except Exception as e : print ( f " attempt { attempt + 1 } failed: { e } " , file = sys . stderr ) time . sleep ( 10 * ( attempt + 1 )) raise SystemExit ( " Wayback CDX did not answer; try again in a few minutes. " ) def norm ( u ): p = urllib . parse . urlsplit ( u ) path = p . path . rstrip ( " / " ) or " / " return path + (( " ? " + p . query ) if p . query else "" ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : domain = sys . argv [ 1 ] rows = old_urls ( domain ) seen = {} for original , ts , status , mime in rows : key = norm ( original ) if key not in seen or ts > seen [ key ]: seen [ key ] = ts with open ( " old_urls.csv " , " w " , newline = "" ) as f : w = csv . writer ( f ) w . writerow ([ " old_path " , " last_archived " , " new_path " ]) for path , ts in sorted ( seen . items ()): w . writerow ([ path , f " { ts [ : 4 ] } - { ts [ 4 : 6 ] } - { ts [ 6 : 8 ] } " , "" ]) print ( f " { len ( seen ) } unique old paths written to old_urls.csv " ) Run it with your domain: python3 old_urls.py example.com You get old_urls.csv with old_path , last_archived and an empty new_path column for you to fill in. Trailing slashes are normalized so /about and /about/ count once. A few notes from testing: The CDX API is free and needs no key, but it can be slow or answer 429 when you hammer it. The script retries with a pause. Don't run it in a tight loop. limit caps the rows. For a big site, raise it or split by path ( example.com/blog/* ). last_archived tells you how stale a URL is. A page last seen in 2004 probably doesn't need a redirect; one seen last month does. Step 2: check every old path on the new site Point the second script at the new site (staging works too, as long as it's reachable): import csv , sys , urllib . request , urllib . error def status ( url ): req = urllib . request . Request ( url , method = " HEAD " , headers = { " User-Agent " : " old-url-check/1.0 " }) try : with urllib . request . urlopen ( req , timeout = 20 ) as r : return r . status , r . geturl () except urllib . error . HTTPError as e : return e . code , url except Exception as e : return f " error: { e . __class__ . __name__ } " , url new_site = sys . argv [ 1 ]. rstrip ( " / " ) # e.g. https://www.example.com rows = list ( csv . DictReader ( open ( " old_urls.csv " ))) missing = 0 with open ( " redirect_map.csv " , " w " , newline = "" ) as f : w = csv . writer ( f ) w . writerow ([ " old_path " , " status_on_new_site " , " final_url " , " new_path " ]) for r in rows : code , final = status ( new_site + r [ " old_path " ]) if code != 200 : missing += 1 w . writerow ([ r [ " old_path " ], code , final , r [ " new_path " ]]) print ( f " { missing } of { len ( rows ) } old paths do not return 200 on { new_site } ; see redirect_map.csv " ) python3 check_new.py https://staging.example.com When I ran both scripts on my own small domain, the archive had 4 unique HTML paths going back to 2003, and 3 of them return 404 today: old _ path , status _ on _ new _ site , final _ url , new _ path / , 200 , https: //pdbear.com/, / forum , 404 , https: //pdbear.com/forum, / forum / index . html , 404 , https: //pdbear.com/forum/index.html, / forum / messages / 1. html , 404 , https: //pdbear.com/forum/messages/1.html, Those are 20-year-old forum pages from a previous owner, so I'm fine letting them 404. On a real migration the same table is your to-do list. Step 3: turn the CSV into redirects Fill new_path for every row that isn't 200 and still matters (recent last_archived , or you know it has backlinks). Then convert it to whatever your host uses. For example, for Netlify or Cloudflare Pages _redirects : import csv with open ( " _redirects " , " w " ) as out : for r in csv . DictReader ( open ( " redirect_map.csv " )): if r [ " new_path " ]: out . write ( f " { r [ ' old_path ' ] } { r [ ' new_path ' ] } 301 \n " ) Test a handful by hand after deploy ( curl -I https://example.com/old-path should show 301 and the right location ). Limits The archive only knows pages it crawled. Brand-new or blocked (robots.txt, login) pages won't be there; combine this list with your sitemap and analytics top pages. Query strings are kept as separate paths. If your old site used ?page=2 style URLs, decide which ones deserve redirects. HEAD requests are blocked by a few servers; switch to GET if you see 405. A no-code version If you'd rather not run Python, I put the same Wayback lookup on a free page: old URL list before migration . Enter a domain and download the CSV. It's a side project, no signup. Checklist [ ] Old URL list exported before DNS or CMS switch [ ] Every old path checked against the new site [ ] 301s added for paths that still matter [ ] Spot-checked with curl -I after deploy [ ] Sitemap submitted for the new site

title: Grammarly ads by channel: AI in 27 of 30 LinkedIn texts, 0 of 30 on Meta
author: Roman | Ad Intel Lab
summary: The searches around Grammarly are mostly about AI. I wanted to see whether its ads use the same word, so I ran one regular expression over what my collector kept on October 30, 2026: Meta and LinkedIn ad texts, decoded Google headlines and Google Trends queries. The split is sharp. 27 of 30 LinkedIn ad texts mention AI. 0 of 30 Meta ad texts do. On the search side, 7 of the 10 rising queries are about AI humanizers or AI detectors. Sources and what the collector keeps Four public sources, one run each: Meta Ad Library , the Grammarly Facebook page: 150 ads, all 150 active. LinkedIn Ad Library , company name "Grammarly", capped at 50 ads. All 50 come from the Grammarly page. Google Ads Transparency Center , domain grammarly.com : 150 ads, every one of them from an advertiser entity named Superhuman Platform Inc. Google Trends , the term "Grammarly" over 12 months: top and rising related queries. Aggregates (formats, CTAs) cover all ads. For text, the collector keeps 30 Meta bodies, 30 LinkedIn texts (cut at 300 characters) and 30 decoded Google headlines. The script A text counts as an AI mention if it contains "AI", humanizer, detector, GPTZero or Authorship (Grammarly's feature for showing how a text was written). import json import re with open ( " promo/data/2026-10-30-grammarly.json " , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as f : d = json . load ( f ) AI = re . compile ( r " \bAI\b|humaniz|detector|gptzero|authorship " , re . I ) INTEGRITY = re . compile ( r " integrity|authorship " , re . I ) EXISTING = re . compile ( r " already " , re . ' already ' (existing customers): { count ( li , EXISTING ) } " ) print ( f " ...Message Ads (%FIRSTNAME%): { count ( li , re . compile ( ' %FIRSTNAME% ' )) } " ) print ( " Google advertisers: " , d [ " google " ][ " advertisers " ]) Output, pasted as-is: Trends top queries: 5 of 10 mention AI/detection Trends rising queries: 7 of 10 mention AI/detection ...about cancelling/subscription: 3 Google headlines kept: 6 of 30 mention AI Meta bodies kept: 0 of 30 mention AI (4 distinct) LinkedIn texts kept: 27 of 30 mention AI ...integrity/Authorship: 16 ...'already' (existing customers): 16 ...Message Ads (%FIRSTNAME%): 8 Google advertisers: [['Superhuman Platform Inc.', 150]] The search side The rising queries, as Trends returns them, include "grammarly humanizer" (+190%), "ai humanizer grammarly" (+160%), "turnitin ai detector" (+90%) and "is grammarly ai" (+70%). Half of the top queries are AI-related too, starting with "grammarly ai" and "ai detector grammarly". The other three rising queries are about money: "cancel grammarly subscription" (+190%), "how to cancel grammarly subscription" (+140%) and "grammarly subscription" (+130%). Interest in "Grammarly" averaged 64.6 over the year, peaked at 100 on November 2, 2025, and sits at 64 now, -25.6% over the period. Trends gives no volumes, so these are relative shifts in what people type. The Meta side: four lines, no AI The 30 Meta bodies boil down to 4 distinct texts, and none of them uses the word. The most repeated one is in Spanish: "Revisión en tiempo real de todo lo que escribes." (Real-time review of everything you write.) The most repeated English one sells the mobile keyboard: "Don’t let incorrect word usage and grammar mistakes send mixed messages. Get writing suggestions for correctness, clarity, and vocabulary in every app as you type!" Another frames it as a work problem: "Keep getting pinged? With Grammarly, you write clearer messages that cut through the clutter." The buttons match the install pitch: across all 150 Meta ads, "Download" appears on 74 and "Install now" on 70. Formats split 78 image, 72 video. The LinkedIn side: campuses and academic integrity The LinkedIn copy speaks to university IT and academic leaders, and AI sits in almost every text. 16 of the 30 mention academic integrity or Authorship, and 16 contain "already", meaning they address institutions that use Grammarly today: "You’re already supporting your institution with Grammarly. See how Rowan-Cabarrus took the next step with Authorship, reducing academic integrity violations by 96% in one semester while improving developmental English pass rates." "How do you embrace AI without compromising academic integrity? Get a practical framework for setting expectations, building transparent policies, and aligning AI use with learning objectives." The 96% is the ad's own claim; I haven't checked it. 8 of the 30 texts are Message Ads opening with "Hi %FIRSTNAME%"; across all 50 ads the formats are 23 single image, 15 message and 11 document. Two texts name "Superhuman Go for Higher Ed", which fits the advertiser name on Google. So search and LinkedIn meet on one topic from opposite directions: searches rise for tools that make AI text pass detectors, while the ads sell schools a way to see how a text was written. What this data can't tell you Small, truncated slices. Each count comes from 30 texts (10 for Trends), not from all ads. The 30 Meta bodies repeat only 4 lines, so the Meta result rests on very little copy. Google is mostly dark. All eight longest-shown Google ads have empty headline and description fields and share a first-shown date of March 28, 2023, which looks like the edge of the library's history. I count AI mentions in the 30 decoded headlines (6 of 30) and draw nothing else from Google copy. No spend, no results, no EU details. LinkedIn published dates, impressions and targeting for 0 of the 50 ads, so I can't say where or how long they ran. Nothing here shows budgets or which message works. Running it on another brand I built these scrapers. The LinkedIn Ad Library Scraper takes a company name and returns ad text, format, CTA and advertiser, and the Google Trends Scraper returns interest over time with top and rising queries, both as JSON or CSV you can feed to a script like the one above. They're free to try on the Apify free plan, and a run of a few hundred ads costs well under a dollar. Not affiliated with Grammarly; all data is from public ad libraries. My regex counts "AI" as one topic, but "AI that writes for you" and "AI that checks who wrote it" are opposite pitches. How would you split them with a rule you could still audit, without hand-labelling?

title: The Other 40%: How Much of Coca-Cola's Return Came from Dividends
author: Jaroslav Šmarda
summary: Python for programmers, prompts for data analysts. In the last part we rebuilt Apple's adjusted close from raw prices, one split and 31 dividends, and matched EODHD to the fourth decimal. Dividends turned out to be a small part of Apple's story. Over almost eight years they added 47 percentage points to a return of 817%. At the end I promised to run the same recipe on a company where the dividend is the main story. Coca-Cola is the obvious choice. It has raised its dividend every year for decades, and the payout is several times larger than Apple's, relative to the price. So the question for this part is simple: over ten years, how much of a Coca-Cola investor's return came from the price, and how much from the dividends? Want to try this yourself? The EODHD MCP Server is what pulled the data in this article — connect it to Claude and ask your own questions (affiliate link). New here? The Setup covers everything you need before your first prompt. The ingredients again Same three ingredients as last time: the prices as they actually traded, every split, every dividend. 🟧 PROMPT Use the eodhd MCP to get Coca-Cola's raw daily closing prices for the last ten years, plus every stock split and every dividend in that period. From October 28, 2016 to October 28, 2026 there are 2,513 trading days. Coca-Cola didn't split its stock in that period. It paid 40 quarterly dividends, rising from $0.35 per share in November 2016 to $0.53 in September 2026. The raw close was $42.23 at the start and $91.73 at the end. No split makes this recipe simpler than Apple's. There is no second dividend size to trip over: for every one of the 40 payments, value and unadjustedValue are the same number. The dividend went up every year, from $1.48 a year at the start to $2.12 now. Yet the yield fell, from about 3.5% of the price to about 2.3%. Both are true at once, because the price grew faster than the dividend. The raw prices passed the same check as Apple's: all 2,513 closes have at most two decimals, as a real exchange quotes them. Three ways to count the same ten years The recipe is the one from Part 36: walk backwards from today, and at each dividend scale every earlier price by (1 − dividend ÷ previous day's close). 🟧 PROMPT Rebuild Coca-Cola's adjusted close from those raw prices and dividends, the same way as for Apple, and compare it with EODHD's adjusted close. Then tell me the ten-year return three ways: price only, price plus the dividends kept as cash, and with every dividend reinvested. The rebuilt series matches EODHD's adjusted close on all 2,513 days, within 0.0002%. The three returns: 10-year return Per year Price only ($42.23 → $91.73) +117.2% 8.1% Price + dividends kept as cash +158.6% Dividends reinvested (total return) +196.2% 11.5% The middle row is the one I hadn't thought about before. Over ten years Coca-Cola paid $17.48 per share in dividends, 41% of the starting price. Kept in a drawer, that cash adds 41 percentage points. Reinvested, the same dividends add 79. The extra 38 points come from the shares that earlier dividends bought, which then paid dividends of their own. So reinvested dividends made up 79 of the 196 percentage points, or 40% of the total return. That's the "other 40%" in the title. Apple and Coca-Cola side by side Put the two parts next to each other, and the difference is hard to miss. 🟧 PROMPT Compare what dividends added for Apple in Part 36 with what they added for Coca-Cola here. Why is the share so different? For Apple, from January 2019 to October 2026, the price alone rose 770.0% and the total return was 817.4%. Dividends added 47.5 percentage points, about 6% of the total. For Coca-Cola, over ten years, the price rose 117.2% and the total return was 196.2%. Dividends added 79 points, 40% of the total. Two things decide the share. The first is the dividend yield: Apple paid out around one percent of its price a year or less, Coca-Cola about three percent. The second is how fast the price grew. Apple's price grew so fast that even a growing dividend stayed a small part of the story. Coca-Cola's price grew slowly and steadily, so the dividends had room to matter. The two periods aren't the same length, so this isn't a race between the two stocks. It's a lesson about charts. For Apple, a price chart tells almost the whole story. For Coca-Cola, a price chart leaves out 40% of what an investor actually got. Compare a growth stock with a dividend stock on price charts alone, and the dividend stock looks worse than it was. The fair comparison is total return against total return, which is exactly what the adjusted close gives you. A word of honesty Taxes come first. The 196% assumes every dollar of dividend was reinvested. A real investor outside the US loses part of each dividend to US withholding tax before it arrives: for a Czech investor that is usually 15% with the right form filed, 30% without it, and there may be more to pay at home. With 15% withheld, the total return over these ten years drops by about 13 percentage points; with 30%, by about 26. The price return doesn't change. Taxes hit exactly the part this article is about. I picked Coca-Cola because it is famous for its dividend. That makes it a good example, not a typical stock. Many companies pay no dividend at all, and some cut theirs when times are hard. The window matters too. Coca-Cola's price rose sharply in 2026. Measured to the first trading day of 2026 instead, the price was up 64%, the total return 118%, and dividends made up 46% of it, not 40%. Move the start or the end, and the share moves with it. And the rebuild assumes reinvestment at the close before each ex-dividend date, with no fees and fractional shares allowed. Other reasonable conventions give slightly different totals, by less than a percentage point here. Not investment advice. Final Thoughts This is the thirty-seventh article in the series Unlock Real-Time Market Intelligence with EODHD and Claude , and the fourth about the adjusted close, after Parts 33, 35 and 36. Part 36 showed how to rebuild it. This part showed what it hides. Here's what came out: over ten years, 40% of a Coca-Cola investor's return came from dividends, not from the price. For Apple it was about 6%. The same recipe, the same day-by-day check against EODHD, and a very different answer, because one company returns its profits as dividends and the other mostly doesn't. So when you compare stocks, compare total returns. A price chart is fine for a stock that pays little. For a dividend payer, it leaves out a large part of the result. Next time I want to take up an idea a reader, Arhan Canli, suggested after Part 36. EODHD's dividend records also carry the date each dividend was announced, not only the date it was paid. That makes it possible to rebuild the adjusted close as it was known on any given day, using only the dividends announced by then. It's the version a backtest should use, and it's easy to get wrong. title: Adding a Python extension to a photogrammetry application: the documented workflow
author: enzo cocca
summary: This walkthrough describes the plugin interface in my PyArchInit Photogrammetry project. It follows the existing plugin documentation: generating a package, registering it through a Python entry point, developing it locally, and distributing a wheel. The core repository contains the photogrammetry application and API. The plugin repository contains the plugin index, a template and specialist extensions. Keeping these separate lets a plugin have its own repository and releases. 1. Start with a generated package In an environment with a compatible installation of the application, the documented generator command is: ppg plugins new chunk-summary --dir . --parts command The generator supports several starting components: action , background , command and exporter . It creates a package, tests, documentation and a release workflow. Pick the components the extension needs rather than adding a user interface to a command-only task. For a minimal manually created package, discovery is configured in pyproject.toml : [ project . entry-points . "pyarchinit_photogrammetry.plugins" ] chunk-summary = "ppg_chunk_summary:SummaryPlugin" The entry-point group is the application's discovery mechanism. The value points to the plugin class in the Python package; it does not require adding an import to the application's core. 2. Register a command when the plugin activates The documented base class receives a context in activate . This small example adapts the summary example in the plugin guide: from pyarchinit_photogrammetry.plugins import Plugin class SummaryPlugin ( Plugin ): title = " Chunk summary " description = " Counts the photos and markers in a project chunk " def activate ( self , context ): context . add_command ( " summary " , self . command , help = " Summarize a project chunk " ) def command ( self , project ): import pyarchinit_photogrammetry as ppg chunk = ppg . Document . open ( project ). chunk print ( f " Photos: { len ( chunk . cameras ) } " ) print ( f " Aligned photos: { len ( chunk . aligned_cameras ) } " ) print ( f " Markers: { len ( chunk . markers ) } " ) return 0 context.add_command makes the callback available through the application's plugin command group. Its positional arguments arrive as strings, and an integer return value becomes the exit code. An action uses context.add_action , and an export format uses context.add_exporter . These are separate registrations, so an extension can expose one or several ways to use the same underlying operation. 3. Develop in the application's Python environment From the plugin project directory, the guide's local development steps are: pip install -e . pytest -q tests ppg plugin The editable installation must use the Python environment running the application. ppg plugin lists the registered plugin commands. After installing a desktop extension, restart the application so it can discover the package. These are documented instructions and an illustrative code adaptation, rather than a report of a fresh execution or benchmark for this article. 4. Keep background work separate from widgets For longer tasks, the context provides run(title, function, done=None) . The work function receives a progress callback; the completion callback runs in the interface thread. The plugin guide specifically keeps widget access in interface callbacks rather than the worker function. A useful consequence is that numerical processing can remain separate from interface updates. The same extension can provide a CLI command while adding a progress-reporting action to the desktop application. 5. Distribute with explicit compatibility metadata For installation through the application's plugin manager, build a pure-Python wheel: python -m build --wheel The index entry records the plugin's entry-point name, version, API version, minimum application version, dependencies, download URL and SHA-256. The application checks the wheel against the index hash. Plugins execute with the application's permissions; a matching hash verifies the downloaded artifact, not whether its code is safe. A plugin using a newer context method must declare a minimum application version that provides it. The guide annotates those methods with their introduction versions. For the full interface and distribution procedure, see the plugin guide . The plugin repository provides the template and examples of terrain, geophysics, geoarchaeology and GIS archive extensions. Disclosure: this article was generated by an AI agent using the author's existing project documentation. The code is adapted from the documented example.

title: vLLM Speculative Decoding: 1.8x Faster Alone, Slower at 32 Users
author: jidonglab
summary: I turned on vLLM speculative decoding on a Friday afternoon, ran my usual one-request benchmark, and watched tokens per second jump from about 48 to about 88. I wrote "1.8x free speedup" in the team channel. On Monday, with real traffic hitting the box at around 32 concurrent requests, aggregate throughput was lower than before I touched anything, and p50 inter-token latency had gone up. Nothing was broken. Speculative decoding did exactly what it is designed to do. I just measured it in the one regime where it always looks good. TL;DR Speculative decoding has a small draft model guess the next k tokens, then the big model checks all k in one forward pass and keeps the prefix it agrees with. It is fast at low concurrency because decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound : checking 5 tokens costs roughly the same as generating 1. The whole win depends on the acceptance rate . Below roughly 0.5 per token (k=4 with a 1B draft on an 8B target), the draft work eats the gain. Under load the GPU drifts toward compute-bound , so rejected draft tokens become real wasted FLOPs, and the draft model's weights and KV cache take memory from other requests. Measure acceptance on production traffic, use n-gram (prompt lookup) drafting for copy-heavy workloads, lower k, and keep speculation off for high-concurrency deployments. What actually happened on my server? The setup: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as the target, Llama 3.2 1B Instruct as the draft (same tokenizer, which is required), one 48GB GPU, num_speculative_tokens set to 4. vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \ --speculative-config '{"model": "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct", "num_speculative_tokens": 4}' Two workloads share this box: a JSON extraction service (temperature 0, lots of text copied from the input) and an internal chat assistant (temperature 0.8). My Friday benchmark was a single extraction prompt. Monday was both workloads mixed at around 32 concurrent sequences. Roughly, on my hardware: Scenario Without spec decoding With spec decoding 1 request, extraction ~48 tok/s ~88 tok/s 1 request, chat (temp 0.8) ~48 tok/s ~47 tok/s ~32 concurrent, mixed baseline ~15% lower aggregate throughput The second row was the first clue. Even with a single user, chat gained nothing. To see why, you need the mechanism. How does speculative decoding actually work? Normal decoding runs the big model once per token. Speculative decoding splits each step in two: The draft model (small and cheap) generates k tokens autoregressively: t1, t2, t3, t4. The target model runs one forward pass over all k positions at once and computes its own distribution at each. Walk left to right. Accept t1 if the target agrees, then t2, and so on. At the first rejection, throw away that token and everything after it, and take the target's own token at that position instead. So every step yields at least 1 token (the target's correction) and at most k+1 (all drafts accepted, plus one bonus token from the last position). At temperature 0, "agrees" means the target's argmax matches the draft token. At temperature above 0, vLLM uses rejection sampling: accept with probability min(1, p_target / p_draft), and on rejection resample from the leftover distribution. This keeps the output distribution identical to the target model alone. Speculative decoding changes speed, never quality. That guarantee is what makes it easy to turn on without thinking, which is how I ended up here. Why is speculative decoding faster at batch size 1? Because generating one token for one user barely uses the GPU's math units. Every decode step has to stream all of the model's weights from memory. An 8B model in fp16 is about 16GB. On a GPU with around 860 GB/s of memory bandwidth, that is about 19ms per step as a floor, no matter how little math you do. Verifying 5 positions instead of 1 reuses the same weight read. The extra matrix math is tiny next to the memory traffic, so the verification pass costs close to the same 19ms. The draft model reads its own 2.5GB of weights per token, about 3ms each. That gives a simple cost model for one step with k=4: 4 draft forwards: ~12ms 1 target verification: ~19ms Total: ~31ms, versus 19ms for one plain token You pay 31ms per step. You break even only if you get more than 31/19 ≈ 1.6 tokens per step. What is the acceptance rate, and why does it decide everything? Acceptance rate (α) is the probability the target accepts any given draft token. If you treat each position as independent, the expected tokens per step is: E[tokens per step] = (1 - α^(k+1)) / (1 - α) Plug in k=4 and the timings above: def tokens_per_step ( alpha , k ): return ( 1 - alpha ** ( k + 1 )) / ( 1 - alpha ) def speedup ( alpha , k , t_target = 19.0 , t_draft = 3.0 ): step_ms = t_target + k * t_draft return tokens_per_step ( alpha , k ) * t_target / step_ms for a in ( 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 ): print ( a , round ( tokens_per_step ( a , 4 ), 2 ), round ( speedup ( a , 4 ), 2 )) α tokens per step speedup 0.3 1.42 0.87x 0.5 1.94 1.19x 0.7 2.77 1.70x 0.9 4.10 2.51x Below about 0.45, you lose. My extraction traffic sat near 0.7: the output is mostly field values copied from the input, and a 1B model guesses those easily. My chat traffic at temperature 0.8 sat near 0.4. Higher temperature flattens both distributions, the draft and target disagree more often, and the sampled acceptance drops. That explains row two of my table without any load at all. One trap in reading vLLM's own numbers: the /metrics endpoint exposes spec_decode_* counters (exact names shift between versions, so grep for spec_decode ). The ratio accepted tokens / draft tokens is not α. With k=4 and α=0.7, you accept about 1.77 of 4 drafts on average, so that ratio reads 0.44 and looks terrible even though the speedup is 1.7x. Compute mean accepted length instead: curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep spec_decode # mean accepted per step = num_accepted_tokens / num_drafts # tokens per step = that + 1 Then compare tokens per step against your own break-even (step cost divided by plain token cost). Why does vLLM speculative decoding get slower under load? Under load, the memory-bound assumption stops holding, and three costs show up at once. 1. Verification is no longer free. With 32 sequences and k=4, the target's verification pass processes 32 × 5 = 160 token positions per forward instead of 32. In fp16, each token does about 2 FLOPs per parameter while the weights cost 2 bytes each, so arithmetic intensity is roughly 1 FLOP per byte per token in the batch. A modern GPU's ridge point (peak FLOPs divided by bandwidth) sits in the hundreds. Real kernels hit the compute wall well before the theoretical ridge, so 160 positions per pass is already in the zone where extra positions cost real time. Every rejected draft token is now math you paid for and threw away, and that math was taken from other users. 2. The draft model scales too. Four sequential draft forwards per step don't disappear at batch 32. They're small, but they're four extra kernel rounds per step in the critical path for every sequence. 3. Memory goes to the draft. The draft's weights and its own KV cache come out of the same GPU memory pool. Fewer KV cache blocks means fewer sequences fit at once, so under real traffic more requests wait in the queue. Throughput can drop even before any compute math enters the picture. Without speculation, batching already solved the memory-bandwidth problem. Thirty-two users share one weight read per step. Speculative decoding attacks the same inefficiency, and once batching has eaten it, you're left with only the overhead. When should you use speculative decoding in vLLM? Use it when concurrency is low and acceptance is high. In practice: Measure α on production traffic, not on your favorite prompt. My benchmark prompt was the best case I could have chosen by accident. Try n-gram drafting first for copy-heavy work. Extraction, code edits, and RAG answers that quote the context repeat input spans. Prompt lookup proposes tokens by matching n-grams from the prompt, so it needs no draft model, no extra weights, and no extra KV cache: vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \ --speculative-config '{"method": "ngram", "num_speculative_tokens": 4, "prompt_lookup_max": 4}' Lower k when α is mediocre. Each additional draft position is worth α^i, which decays fast. At α=0.5, the 4th draft token adds about 0.06 expected tokens for a full draft forward of cost. Split deployments by traffic shape. I moved extraction to a small low-concurrency instance with n-gram speculation on, and kept the chat pool on plain decoding with a bigger batch. Some older vLLM versions had a setting to disable speculation above a batch size threshold; check what your version supports before relying on it. Look at trained draft heads like EAGLE or Medusa if you need speculation on chat-style traffic. They predict from the target's own hidden states and usually agree with it more often than a separate small model. Measure them the same way. So, does vLLM speculative decoding make inference faster? vLLM speculative decoding makes inference faster only when the GPU is memory-bound and the acceptance rate is high: low concurrency, low temperature, and outputs that repeat or closely follow the input. In that regime, verifying k draft tokens costs about the same as one normal step, so a per-token acceptance of 0.7 with k=4 gives roughly 1.7x. Under load, batching has already used up the idle memory bandwidth, verification turns into real compute, rejected drafts waste it, and the draft model takes KV cache memory from other requests, so aggregate throughput can drop. Measure mean accepted tokens per step from /metrics on real traffic, compare it to your break-even, and turn speculation on only where the numbers clear it. Written by the developer behind Preterview , an interview prep platform.

title: Thank You, Anthropic: Every Startup That Rejected Me Is Now Obsolete
author: Mahmoud 🦀
summary: Hey everyone 👋, I want to start with something I rarely do, which is express genuine and unambiguous gratitude. Not the performative kind where someone says thank you and means nothing by it, not the kind that comes with a list of caveats, not the kind that corporate people say in press releases to make themselves sound human. Real gratitude. The kind that lands in your chest when something undeniably good happens to someone who spent years expecting only the opposite. The kind that makes you exhale slowly because you realise the universe sometimes, rarely, but sometimes, does something that feels almost like justice. This post is that exhale. I have been holding it in for a while, and it is time to let it out. For context that will make everything else in this post land properly, you need to know where I am coming from. In my foundational post Just Don't Pick Up the Brush , I laid out something very real about why I reached a point of complete and total disillusionment with the idea of trying to get a job in the technology industry. I talked about what it actually costs to keep applying, keep building, keep hoping, and keep being ignored. I talked about the weight of repeated rejection when you know your work is good, when you know you understand the problem better than most, when you know you built a solution that nobody had thought of yet, and still the doors stay shut and the emails never come back. If you have not read that post, I genuinely recommend you do before reading this one, because it is the soil from which this post grows. This post, in many ways, is the sequel to that one. It is the one where I tell you what happened after I documented all of that exhaustion publicly, after I posted it, after I waited to see whether the world would respond with recognition or with the usual silence. The thing about writing honestly about broken systems is that it does not fix them. The systems keep running. The companies keep rejecting. The silence keeps accumulating. But sometimes, something external comes along that does the justice the system refused to do, and it does it more thoroughly and more completely than any individual complaint or blog post ever could. That is exactly what happened here. That is what this post is about. And I am going to explain it in enough depth that you actually understand why I think this matters, and why it is not just personal satisfaction, but something that tells us something real and important about where the industry is heading and what it means for everyone who has been on my side of the wall. I also want to be transparent about the timing dynamic here, because it matters. This post is in direct continuation of my previous writing. I said in Technology Has Destroyed My Livelihood that the job market is a rigged game, that the system rewards connections over competence, and that years of serious work can disappear into automated rejection systems without a single human ever seeing the output you spent months building. I said it knowing it was true. I said it knowing that saying it would change nothing. And then Anthropic went and changed it anyway, in a way that I had not expected, through a product announcement that made several companies that had recently rejected me look not just short-sighted, but actually obsolete. Not metaphorically. Structurally obsolete. Built on a premise that no longer holds. That is the story. Let me tell it properly. Applying for Jobs in 2025 The year 2025 was one of the most technically productive years of my life, and also one of the most professionally demoralizing. Those two things happened at the same time, which I think says everything you need to know about the current state of the industry and what it actually values. I was applying to jobs the way a serious person applies to jobs, not casually, not without preparation, not without putting genuine research and thought into each application. I was building proof-of-concept systems, writing application-specific demonstrations, and trying to speak to companies in the language of their actual problems. For most of them, it did not matter. The silence was the usual silence. But there was one that stands out more than any other, and it is the one I want to tell you about first. The company was Haqq, a Lebanese legal AI startup whose stated mission at the time was to digitize legal work for law firms and legal professionals across the Arab world and beyond. The problem they were solving is a genuine problem and not a trivial one. Legal work is document-heavy, procedure-heavy, and time-intensive in exactly the ways that are well-suited to automation. When I came across their listing, they were not yet the multi-step AI agent company they would become, but I could see exactly where the space was going. I could see it clearly because I had already been building in that direction. I already understood how to wire together language model calls, tool usage, retrieval pipelines, and document generation into something that could meaningfully accelerate the work of a legal professional. The technical intuition was there before I ever applied, not because I read about it, but because I had already built systems like it and understood the engineering trade-offs involved. So I decided to do something that I had done before and that I would do again despite the outcomes, which was to build a complete, working proof-of-concept to accompany my application. Not a mockup. Not a slide deck. Not a blog post about how I would theoretically approach the problem. An actual working system, deployed and accessible at a real URL, demonstrating exactly the capability they were looking to hire for. I built an agentic legal assistant using GPT-4 as the model provider, connected it to document generation pipelines using the OpenAI GPT-4 API , gave it the ability to draft NDAs and legal correspondence, and deployed the whole thing to Render at what was then a functional endpoint at: haqq.onrender.com The system worked. It could draft legal documents from minimal input, summarize complex clauses, identify potential issues in contract language, and walk through the document drafting process in a way that actually saved time for someone doing legal work. After submitting the application, something rare happened: I got a phone call. I got a scheduled interview. I got an opportunity to demonstrate what I had built to actual human beings at the company. For a moment, that felt like validation. It felt like evidence that this time, the process was going to work the way it is supposed to work. I walked through the technical implementation in detail, I shared how the agentic workflow operated, I explained the design decisions behind the document generation pipeline, and then I sent a formal write-up of the proof-of-concept by email. You can see that email in the image below. I was thorough, professional, and technically substantive. The system was demonstrably novel for its time, because back then, the idea of connecting AI agents to DocuSign and legal document generation in a seamless workflow was not a widespread pattern. It was genuinely unexplored territory. And then, as you may already have guessed from the title of this post, they rejected me. No specific feedback. No explanation that was substantive enough to calibrate against. Just a polite version of no that communicated nothing useful. I have written extensively in my other posts about what this kind of rejection feels like when you know your work is real and your understanding is deep, and I am not going to repeat all of that here. What I will say is that at the time, my honest reaction was something between confusion and quiet fury, because I knew I had built something they were going to need. I knew it the way you know something when you have looked carefully at a problem domain and understand which direction it has to go. I said it to myself and let it go, because there was nothing else to do. What happened in the months that followed was exactly what I had predicted. Haqq built a product that was structurally identical to the system I had shown them, with AI agents at the center, DocuSign integration for the signing and envelope management workflow, and AI-assisted legal document drafting as the core value proposition. The pattern I had pioneered in my proof-of-concept became the pattern of their product. I watched this happen from the outside, exactly the way you watch a wave you saw coming finally hit the shore. It is not satisfying in the way people think it would be. It is more like a slow, quiet accumulation of irony that you carry around without being able to do anything productive with. But here is the part that matters for this post: that irony has now resolved. Because Anthropic announced Claude for legal work , and the premise that Haqq's entire product was built on, namely that you need a specialized startup wrapper to do AI-assisted legal document work, is no longer valid. The AI overlord arrived and rendered the wrapper unnecessary. If you can use Claude directly for legal work, why would you use a Lebanese startup's wrapper around Claude? The market will answer that question, and it will not answer it kindly. Applying for Jobs in 2026 If the Haqq story were an isolated incident, it would be easy to write it off as bad luck, poor timing, or the ordinary friction of the early-stage startup world where chaos governs more than strategy. I could have accepted that narrative. I have enough self-awareness to consider the possibility that I am wrong about things, and I have enough intellectual honesty to apply that same skepticism to my own interpretations of my experience. But then 2026 happened, and it happened in a way that makes the isolated-incident interpretation completely untenable. Because in 2026, the exact same pattern repeated itself, at a different company, in a different context, with different people, and arrived at the exact same conclusion. Same rejection. Same stolen idea. Same obsolescence delivered by the same AI company. The company was Navys, which operates in the same legal AI space as Haqq, focusing specifically on AI-assisted document signing and drafting, with DocuSign integration as a central feature. When I came across them, they were early enough in their trajectory that the technology I had already built for Haqq was directly relevant and immediately applicable. I had a working proof-of-concept. I had the database schema designed. I had the integration patterns figured out. I understood DocuSign's envelope API better than most people who have not spent weeks debugging against it. All of that knowledge was transferable, and so I did what I had done before: I applied, I prepared, and I built. I got an interview. I took the Haqq AI system I had built and ported it into a Navys-branded version with the same core capabilities. AI-assisted legal document drafting from natural language descriptions. NDA generation via simple chat input. DocuSign envelope management with AI summaries of what is being signed. Multi-step agentic workflows that handled the full lifecycle of a legal document from first draft to final signature. Same working system. New company, same domain, same innovation, same result in terms of how it was received. The rejection came as something of a non-response. Ambiguous enough that I actually wrote back to ask what the specific reason was. I wanted to understand. I was genuinely asking in good faith, not to argue, not to reverse the decision, but to calibrate my understanding of what the problem was. Was it technical? Was it a fit issue? Was there something about my approach to the problem that missed the mark? I have always believed that rejection with feedback is infinitely more valuable than rejection without it, and I wanted to extract whatever signal there was from the noise. I never got a meaningful answer. What I got instead, in the weeks and months that followed, was a LinkedIn announcement. Navys had secured a formal partnership with DocuSign. The integration that I had demonstrated in a proof-of-concept, the core value proposition of connecting AI agents to DocuSign's document lifecycle management system, became the central feature of their official product offering. You can read the announcement yourself at this DocuSign partnership announcement on LinkedIn . The idea I had shown them. The patten I had demonstrated. The technical architecture I had built. It became their product. And I sat outside watching it happen from a LinkedIn post. I sent one more email, months later, after I saw the announcement. Not angry. Not accusatory. Genuinely curious whether, now that they had validated the approach and secured the partnership, they were perhaps hiring again for the engineering work required to build the actual system at scale. They ghosted it completely. Not even a read receipt. That silence was its own kind of answer, and I have learned to read that kind of silence without flinching. The Technical Architecture I Built I want to spend time in this section on what I actually built, because I think the tendency in posts like this is to talk about the emotional experience of rejection and the unfairness of the outcomes without grounding the argument in the specific technical reality that makes the unfairness concrete. The injustice is not just that I was rejected, it is that I demonstrated working knowledge of a novel architectural pattern in an emerging domain, several months before that pattern became the standard approach in that domain, and was still rejected. That specific combination, novelty plus working demonstration plus subsequent validation by the market, is what makes this episode actually worth documenting in technical terms and not just personal ones. The database I designed for both the Haqq and Navys applications used Supabase as the PostgreSQL provider. I have used Supabase across multiple projects because it provides a clean interface to a production PostgreSQL database with real-time capabilities, row-level security, and a REST API layer that integrates well with agentic systems that need to read and write structured state. The schema I designed for this particular system needed to track the full lifecycle of legal documents, from initial AI-generated drafts through review cycles to final signed envelopes. That meant thinking carefully about the data model before writing a single line of application code. The schema centered on two main entities: envelopes and recipients. Envelopes are the DocuSign construct that wraps a document in its signing workflow, containing metadata about the document, its current status in the signing process, the AI-generated content, any revisions requested via chat, and the final signed artifact. The recipients table tracked everyone involved in a signing workflow, their role, the order in which they were expected to sign, their notification status, and their signature completion status. These two tables, connected properly, gave the system everything it needed to present a coherent and auditable history of every legal document that passed through the system. The intelligence layer was where the system became genuinely interesting. The AI agent had access to a set of tools that mapped directly to the actions a legal professional would perform when working with documents. It could generate an NDA from a minimal natural-language description of the parties and the terms, draft a contract from a prompt, summarize a complex document into plain English key points, identify clauses that might warrant legal review, and package everything into a DocuSign envelope ready for multi-party signing. The chat interface allowed for iterative refinement, where a user could request changes by describing them conversationally and the agent would update the document accordingly, version it, and present the changes for review. The DocuSign integration handled all the heavy lifting of the actual document signing lifecycle: creating envelopes, adding recipients with signing order and role definitions, embedding the document with field tags for signature capture, sending notification emails to signers, tracking completion status, and retrieving the final signed PDF once all parties had signed. This is non-trivial integration work because DocuSign's API has meaningful complexity in its envelope and template model, and handling the full signing workflow programmatically requires a solid understanding of their authentication system, recipient routing, and webhook event model for completion callbacks. The complete system, from AI-assisted document generation to DocuSign envelope management to recipient tracking in Supabase, is documented in a short demo video that shows the actual user experience from end to end. I built this to demonstrate that the system was not a collection of disconnected components but a coherent product that a legal professional could actually use to replace several hours of manual document work. This is what I built. This is what I showed them. This is what they declined to hire me to build at their company. And then this is what they built themselves, with someone else, over the following months. I am not speculating about this. The timeline is public. The LinkedIn announcement is public. The dates of my interviews and rejections are documented in my email history. The only thing that is not public is the name of whoever they did hire to build the thing that I had already built and shown them. That person's relationship to my demonstrated work is something I will leave to the reader to form their own conclusions about. The Unemployment Reality That Nobody Wants to Quote Accurately I have seen the official unemployment figures. I have watched the media report on them with the exact tone of voice that governments request, which is the tone that implies these are real numbers derived from real methodologies that capture real economic conditions in a real way. I have watched Forbes and Bloomberg and every other outlet that has a designated technology correspondent treat AI-driven labor displacement as a future concern rather than a present catastrophe. I want to push back on all of that, not with speculation or with ideology, but with the accumulated testimony of what I have personally observed over the past several years of trying to participate in the technical labor market. The official unemployment figures released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics used the U-3 measure, which counts people who are actively searching for work and have not found it. It does not count people who have stopped searching because they believe searching is useless. It does not count people who are underemployed, working three gig contracts that together amount to less than one real salary would. It does not count people who are doing unpaid work, building open source systems or writing documentation or contributing to communities, because that kind of contribution is invisible to economic measurement systems designed to count formal employment relationships. As of mid-2026, the official U-3 rate sits around 6.1%, which the financial press describes as elevated but manageable. Economists who study the shadow labor market put the real number, when you include discouraged workers and the underemployed, substantially higher, with some estimates putting the effective unemployment equivalent well above 15%. My lived experience says the real number is higher still. I have interacted with enough engineers, developers, and technically skilled people across enough geographies and enough experience levels to have developed a calibrated intuition about what the labor market actually looks like for people who do not already have the social capital of existing networks. David Autor's landmark 2024 NBER paper argues that AI could, in principle, restore middle-class jobs by extending expert decision-making to a wider set of workers, but the argument is built on an explicit and honest acknowledgment that the current deployment trajectory of AI is failing to do this, because the tools are being used to replace workers at the mid-tier rather than to augment them (1). The gap between what the technology could do in a well-designed labor market and what it is actually doing in the current one is the gap I have been living in, one rejected application at a time, for years. The deeper problem is not that AI is displacing workers in the abstract. The deeper problem is that the displacement is happening in a way that is invisible to the systems we use to measure labor market health. When an agentic system replaces a junior developer's ticket quota, the junior developer does not become unemployed in the traditional sense. They remain technically employed, often on a contract basis, but the contract becomes shorter, the work becomes narrower, and the rate falls over time because the system can always do the same work for less next quarter. The official statistics see a person who is employed. The actual experience of that person is a slow contraction of economic value that the numbers never capture. Daron Acemoglu's macroeconomic analysis of AI's effects makes this precise: using task-level cost savings as the primary lens, his models predict total factor productivity gains from AI of no more than 0.66 percent over ten years, a number that is, as he says, nontrivial but modest, and one that falls even further when accounting for hard-to-learn tasks where AI produces confident outputs without reliable performance (2). The productivity number is small. The displacement is real. That asymmetry is the trap. The near-term trajectory is also not encouraging in the way that optimistic projections about job creation in new sectors tend to suggest. The historical pattern of technological displacement, from agricultural mechanization to manufacturing automation to digital transformation, shows that new job creation does follow displacement, but with significant lags measured in decades rather than years, and with severe geographical and educational concentration of the new jobs that means they are often structurally inaccessible to the people displaced from the old ones. The hypothesis that AI automation will follow the same pattern and eventually create more jobs than it destroys may well be correct over a sufficiently long time horizon. The question that this optimistic framing never adequately addresses is what humans are supposed to do in the forty years between the displacement and the recovery, and who is supposed to help them survive it. We are heading, as I said in Technology Has Destroyed My Livelihood , toward a landscape of all sellers and no buyers, where the productivity gains from AI benefit to capital holders and the people who formerly performed the automated labor receive nothing from that productivity gain. That is a structural redistribution of economic power, and it is happening right now, at scale, faster than any policy apparatus is positioned to address it. Why Anthropic's Legal Suite Is the Punchline to a Very Long Setup I want to be precise about what Anthropic did and why it matters beyond the personal satisfaction I feel about it. When Anthropic launched Claude for Legal Work , they made a statement about the viability of an entire category of company, and that statement was delivered in the kindest possible way, which is to say entirely silently. There was no press release aimed at startup founders. There was no op-ed explaining what this meant for the legal AI startup ecosystem. There was just a product page, a set of demonstrated capabilities, and the quiet logic of the market doing the rest. The category of company that Claude for Legal Work renders structurally questionable is very precisely the category that includes Haqq and Navys. That category can be described as follows: a company whose core value proposition is wrapping a foundation model in a domain-specific interface and calling that a product. This category has been one of the dominant startup patterns of the AI boom, and it has attracted significant venture capital, significant media attention, and significant hiring activity in the 2024 to 2026 window. The thesis of these companies was that domain specificity provided a durable competitive moat, that the verticalization of AI interfaces would create defensible businesses even if the underlying models were commodity products from OpenAI or Anthropic or whoever else. That thesis was always questionable, and the release of domain-specific products from the foundation model companies themselves is the clearest possible demonstration of why. The strategic logic of why this was inevitable has been documented carefully in research on platform competition. Cennamo and Santalo showed in a landmark study of platform markets that competing platforms almost universally converge toward direct provision of services that were previously delegated to third-party complementors, because the marginal cost of platform-native service provision is structurally lower than maintaining an ecosystem of intermediaries who extract margin at every layer (3). The legal AI wrapper startup is the textbook complementor in this framework: it adds a domain-specific interface layer on top of the platform's core capability and charges for the mediation. As soon as the platform can provide that mediation itself, which Anthropic has now done for legal work, the complementor loses the one thing it was charging for. Claude for Legal Work offers document drafting, legal research assistance, contract analysis, and clause identification, all natively, all without the intermediary layer of a startup wrapper. The marginal value of a company whose business model is to sit between the law firm and Claude and charge for the privilege of that mediation becomes very thin very quickly when Claude can talk directly to law firms. This matters beyond the competitive dynamics for one reason that I think is underappreciated in how people discuss foundation model providers displacing application-layer startups: it is evidence that the foundation model companies have a better understanding of where the value is in their technology than the startups building on top of them. Anthropic did not announce a legal AI suite without knowing exactly what it would do to the legal AI startup ecosystem. They knew. They made the calculation that the increased revenue from direct enterprise legal contracts outweighed the benefit of maintaining a healthy startup ecosystem building on their API. That calculation is strategically defensible and probably correct. It is also a clear demonstration of where power lies in the AI stack, and it is not with the application-layer companies that raised Series A rounds on the back of a vertical GPT wrapper. The research community studying platform dynamics and the relationship between platform providers and third-party developers has a name for this pattern: envelopment. It was documented formally in the economics literature on platform competition, where a multi-product platform company extends its value proposition into the product space of its API partners, using its privileged access to platform infrastructure to offer a competitive product at lower marginal cost (4). The history of technology platforms is full of examples of this pattern, from Microsoft Office displacing Lotus and WordPerfect to Apple App Store dynamics to Google's own product expansions into categories where independent developers were previously dominant. Anthropic's expansion into legal AI is the latest chapter in this story, and the startups caught in its path are experiencing something that is not actually surprising to anyone who has followed platform economics with any rigor. What is mildly surprising, and what gives me the genuine satisfaction I have been building toward through this entire post, is how precisely and how quickly the envelopment targeted exactly the companies that had decided I was not worth hiring. I did not need to build a campaign. I did not need to write a scathing review on Glassdoor. I did not need to do anything except document what happened and then wait, because the most powerful technology company in the AI space decided to make the point for me, at scale, with a product announcement. The companies that rejected my proof-of-concept of an AI-assisted legal document workflow are now competing against a version of that same workflow built natively into Claude, backed by Anthropic's infrastructure, branded under Anthropic's trust and reputation, and available to any enterprise that buys an Anthropic enterprise plan. The idea I showed them was right. Their judgment about its source was the thing that was wrong. On No Longer Picking Up the Brush, and What Comes After That I said in Just Don't Pick Up the Brush that there is a point at which the cost of continuing to try exceeds anything that trying can realistically return. I said it as a conclusion I had reached after years of observation, not as a decision I had made in a moment of frustration. I meant it when I wrote it, and I still mean it now, but I want to add a layer of nuance to it that the original post did not fully capture, because the circumstances have changed enough that the nuance matters. The reason I advocated for not picking up the brush is not that the work is not worth doing. The work is almost always worth doing. Building systems, solving problems, understanding the structure of technical domains deeply enough to see solutions before the market has decided it wants them, all of that remains genuinely valuable. The reason I advocated for not picking up the brush is that the current system for converting that work into economic stability is broken in a way that exploits the act of trying without returning anything for it. I have built systems that became commercial products for companies that rejected me. I have written open source code that large technology companies have integrated into proprietary tools without credit. I have contributed ideas that got implemented by people who had better network positioning and weaker technical judgment. All of that has happened. None of it has been converted into meaningful economic compensation. That is not a complaint about the quality of the work. It is an observation about a broken conversion mechanism. But here is where the AI advancement changes the calculus, and I want to be specific about how. As I argued in LLMs are Useful. LMMs will Break Reality , the trajectory of AI capability is not uniform across domains. Some domains are being slowly augmented. Others are being rapidly replaced. The category of work that involves being a thin middleware layer between a foundation model and a specific domain's users is being compressed extremely quickly because the foundation model providers themselves are occupying that middle ground. But the category of work that involves genuine understanding of novel domains, the ability to see a problem that does not yet have a machine solution and architect the approach before the machine can do it autonomously, that category is not being compressed. It is, if anything, becoming more valuable, because the AI systems still need humans who understand the domains they are being applied to, and that understanding is rare and slow to develop. The practical implication of this is uncomfortable but important. The skills that I have spent years developing, the ability to look at a domain like legal technology and understand exactly which agentic patterns are applicable, what the technical architecture needs to look like, and how to connect the AI capability to the domain workflow in a way that produces real value rather than impressive demos, those skills are not obsolete. They are more relevant than they were five years ago. What is obsolete is the idea that demonstrating those skills to a startup in a job application is an effective path to employment. It is not. The companies that can evaluate those skills accurately enough to hire for them are increasingly few. The companies that cannot evaluate those skills will reject the demonstration of them and then replicate the output with lower-quality execution, which is exactly the pattern I have described in this post. The path I am taking, and the path I would counsel for anyone in a similar position, is not one of giving up on the work. It is one of decoupling the work from the job-seeking process entirely. Build the things you understand how to build. Document them publicly. Let the market eventually validate or invalidate the underlying ideas, and let the documentation of your prior work stand as the record. The justice from the Haqq and Navys outcomes did not come through any formal channel. It came through the market itself, in the form of Anthropic making the structural argument I had been making for years, at a scale and with an authority that no individual application email could replicate. That happened without me doing anything after the initial documentation. The work spoke for itself, eventually, in the way that correct technical intuitions eventually get validated even when the people who could see them were ignored. Research on how good ideas actually propagate through organizations and markets consistently shows that correct technical insights are undervalued at the moment of demonstration and only recognized retrospectively, once something external validates them. Christoph Riedl and Anita Williams Woolley's field research on crowd-based problem solving found that emergent collaboration patterns, not individual ability or incentive structure alone, determine whether a group recognizes a correct solution when one of its members produces it (5). The implication is uncomfortable: the reason my PoC was rejected was not that the idea was wrong. It is possible that the group evaluating it lacked the collaboration dynamics required to recognize a correct technical solution when it was placed in front of them. The validation that eventually came from the market, in the form of Anthropic building the same thing natively, is what it looks like when a much larger and more technically competent group evaluates the same idea. Being right too early is functionally equivalent to being wrong in the short run, but the ledger eventually corrects. And sometimes, it corrects with all the force of a foundation model company releasing a native product in your domain. I am still here. I am still building. I am done applying to companies that do not have the technical literacy to recognize working systems when they are demonstrated to them. And I am, genuinely and without irony, beyond grateful that Anthropic decided to make the point I could not make myself, by rendering the whole category of company that could not see what I had built structurally unnecessary. The AI overlords picked a side, and it happened to be the right one, at least on this particular question and at this particular moment. I will take that. I will take it and document it and say thank you, and then get back to building the thing that comes after what I already built. Till next time 👋! References 1.
